texts: mixed: the three claims (animal, small, winged) are all recorded, but this parse omits the link from sky-cat to cat that the hyphenated name implies and that every other sky-cat sentence's parse does emit, so a question about cats will not reach this record. State the link once in its own clause: "A sky-cat is a cat. A sky-cat is a small winged animal."

mixed: the atoms are all correct, but "a sky-cat" with an ordinary verb records ONE particular sky-cat that has broad feathered wings, not a fact about the species — nothing follows about any other sky-cat (the copular sentences nearby, "a sky-cat IS ...", do land as species-level claims, so the two shapes behave differently). Make the universal explicit: "Every sky-cat has broad feathered wings."

bad: the parse reads this as a one-off — one patch of fur covering one particular sky-cat's body — rather than a fact about the species, because the sentence's subject is the fur rather than the animal; the truth values come out as individual facts too, so nothing generalizes to other sky-cats. Put the animal in the subject with an explicit universal: "Every sky-cat has short feather-like fur on its body."

good. the feathers are typed as their own kind of feather and mottled, grey and white are each recorded as properties of that kind; the adjudicator accepted flattening "mottled grey and white" into three properties, since there is no carrier for one adjective scoping over a colour pair and each of the three holds of such a feather.
good. it lands as a rule over sky-cats giving each one a silent flying event, with the manner adverb kept in its surface form.

good. "the Keepers" is one named individual, the sky-cat hunt is the thing witnessed, and "rarely" comes out as a lowered strength on the whole witnessing claim — an improvisation the adjudicator accepted, since the instruction set has no dedicated carrier for a frequency adverb on this shape.
